In a recent development, someone doesn’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it. Having the right gear really helps, though, and that creates a wellspring of great gifting opportunities. The HORL3 Cruise holds a knife against a magnet at a fixed 15- or 20-degree angle while a diamond disc rolls along the edge. The ThermoWorks Thermapen Nano gets a reading in about 0.4 seconds, so anyone can stop guessing when a roast is done. The Challenger Bread Pan traps steam under a tall cast-iron lid, the same trick bakeries pull off with steam-injected ovens. Every pick below works on that principle, helping the home cook elevate their kitchen experience.

Industry observers note that there are dozens and dozens of gifts here, grouped by category. Jump to: precision and measurement, knives and sharpening, pans and cookware, coffee, tea and drinks, baking and from scratch, countertop appliances, plus sauces and cookbooks.

Seasoning a thick steak with a typical pepper grinder takes a lot of twisting. The MÄNNKITCHEN Pepper Cannon uses hardened high-carbon stainless steel burrs spinning on a drive shaft supported by two bearings inside a body milled from a solid block of anodized aluminum. MÄNNKITCHEN claims 10 times the output of top-rated mills, which it describes as seven cranks instead of 70. You set the grind from 8 to 60+ mesh with an adjuster on the base that clicks into spring-loaded detents. The hopper holds half a cup of peppercorns, and a removable cup underneath catches up to a third of a cup of ground pepper, which is handy when a rub calls for a measured amount.

A big mixing bowl tends to hide a kitchen scale’s display right when you need to read it. On the OXO Good Grips 11 lb Stainless Steel Food Scale with Pull-Out Display, the readout sits on a tray that slides out from the base, clear of whatever’s on the platform, then tucks back in for storage. It weighs up to 11 pounds (5 kilograms), and a meter on the display reveals how much capacity you have left as you add ingredients. The display has an optional backlight, and the stainless steel platform lifts off so you can wash it by hand.

Sous vide cooking holds a water bath at the exact temperature you want your food to finish at, so a steak can sit in it and stay medium-rare instead of drifting toward well-done. The Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 heats that bath with an 1,100-watt element and circulates 8 liters of water per minute, and Anova rates it to hold within 0.2°F anywhere from 32°F to 197°F. A two-line touchscreen on the cooker indicates time and temperature, and dual-band Wi-Fi lets you start or check a cook from your phone. Anova gives it an IPX7 water-resistance rating, and the clamp adjusts and detaches to fit different pots.

Recent findings suggest that thermoWorks has closed out the Thermapen One, and the Thermapen Nano took its place this year. ThermoWorks rates the Nano’s fixed thermocouple probe for a full reading in 0.4 seconds and accuracy within 0.5°F between -4°F and 248°F, a window that covers everything from rare beef to pulled pork. Two magnets built into the body let it ride on the side of the fridge or range hood, and the display rotates a full 360 degrees, so the numbers read right-side up whichever hand you hold it in. It’s IP67 rated, runs roughly 1,000 hours on one AAA battery, and comes with a five-year warranty and a NIST-traceable calibration certificate.

A fast thermocouple thermometer doesn’t have to cost triple digits. TempPro, the brand formerly known as ThermoPro, builds a thermocouple sensor into the TempSwift Pro TP622 and rates it for a 0.1-second response time and accuracy within 0.5°F across -58°F to 572°F. That high end reaches past meat into frying oil and candy-making territory. The backlit display auto-rotates 180 degrees for left- or right-handed use, and the thermometer wakes up when you lift it and goes to sleep after 90 seconds of sitting still. It carries an IP65 water-resistance rating and runs on a single AAA battery.

It has been revealed that the Combustion Predictive Thermometer (2nd Gen) is built around the question people actually ask during a roast: how much longer? Its probe carries eight sensors along its length, so the app can show the core, the surface and the air temperature around the food at the same time. Combustion’s prediction engine uses that heat-flow data to estimate the time remaining, and a feature it calls TrueCore reports the lowest internal reading even if you didn’t hit the center. Combustion rates the upper half of the probe to 900°F, so it can stay in a roast under the broiler or on the grill. Bluetooth reaches more than 330 feet in open air, and Wi-Fi requires a separate booster accessory.

Industry observers note that freehand sharpening is hard mostly because holding a steady angle is hard. The HORL3 Cruise takes that job off your hands: a magnetic block holds the knife at either 15 or 20 degrees, and you roll a wheel with a diamond disc back and forth along the edge. The other end of the roller carries a stainless steel honing disc to straighten and refine the edge you just ground. The Cruise’s body is made from ocean-bound recycled plastic, and HORL builds it in Germany. If the person you’re shopping for would rather have wood on the counter, the $179 HORL3 uses an oak or walnut body and swaps in an interchangeable ceramic disc.

Sources indicate that STEELPORT forges its 8-inch Chef Knife from a single billet of American 52100 carbon steel in Portland, Oregon, then heat treats the edge and spine differently. The company notes the edge ends up around 65 HRC, hard enough to take and hold a fine edge, while the spine stays below 30 HRC so the blade as a whole is less brittle. The handle is resin-stabilized Oregon bigleaf maple burl, and a magnetic walnut sheath comes in the box. Carbon steel picks up a patina and can rust, so wipe it dry after every wash. STEELPORT covers the knife with a lifetime warranty and sharpens it free for as long as you own it.

Sources indicate that A knife that suddenly feels dull often has an edge that’s just rolled over, and a few passes on a honing rod push it back into line between real sharpenings. STEELPORT’s 12-Inch Oval Ceramic Honing Rod does that with a fine-grit ceramic surface over a steel core. The oval cross-section is there for contact, and STEELPORT says it puts more of the blade against the rod than a round one does. The rod measures 17 inches overall with a 5-inch contoured walnut handle and a finger guard, and it weighs 12 ounces. Ceramic can crack if it hits a tile floor, so give it a hook or its own drawer slot.

Shun builds the Classic 8-Inch Chef’s Knife around a VG-MAX steel core clad in 34 layers of stainless Damascus on each side, which is where the rippled pattern on the blade comes from. The core is hardened to 60-61 on the Rockwell scale and hand-sharpened to about 16 degrees per side, a fine edge that slices through onions and herbs cleanly. The full-tang blade sits in a D-shaped black PakkaWood handle, and the whole knife weighs 7.5 ounces. Shun makes it in Seki, Japan. A hard, thin edge like this one is happiest on a wood or plastic board, and it shouldn’t go anywhere near bones or frozen food.

In a recent development, softer stainless steel is quicker to bring back to a sharp edge, and that’s part of the appeal of the Made In 8-Inch Chef Knife. It’s fully forged in Thiers, France, from nitrogen-treated X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58+ HRC, so a few passes on a whetstone or rolling sharpener refresh it. Made In grinds the edge asymmetrically, with a 14-degree primary bevel on one side and a 4-degree polishing bevel on the other, for 18 degrees total. The blade actually measures 8.5 inches and the knife weighs 7 ounces. If you order directly from Made In, the company will engrave it for $30 more, but engraved knives can’t be returned.

Someone outfitting a first real kitchen needs a handful of good knives more than a block with 15 slots. The Cangshan N1 Series 6-Piece Knife Block Set forges its blades from German X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58 HRC, a steel that’s easy to touch up at home. The N1’s signature is its patented all-metal hollow handle, which runs straight out of the blade, so there are no wood or plastic scales to crack or loosen. Cangshan sells the set under more than one model number, so check the knife list on the listing before you order.

Tojiro has renamed its long-running DP line to Classic, but the F-808 210mm gyuto itself didn’t change. It’s a san mai blade, with a VG10 stainless core hardened to about 60 HRC sandwiched between softer stainless outer layers that add toughness around the hard cutting steel. The 50/50 double-bevel edge suits right- and left-handed cooks equally, and the Western-style handle has a full tang, a stainless bolster and three rivets, so it’ll feel familiar to anyone coming from a German knife. Tojiro makes it in Tsubame-Sanjo, Japan. The edge measures 212 millimeters and the knife weighs 7.2 ounces.

Learning to sharpen on a stone starts with two grits, and the King KW-65 puts both on one block. The 1000-grit side does the sharpening and raises a fresh edge, then the 6000-grit side polishes it. It’s a soaking stone, so you submerge it for a couple of minutes before you start and keep it wet while you work. The muddy slurry that builds up on the surface helps it cut, so leave it there rather than rinsing it away mid-session. The stone measures about 7.3 by 2.5 by 1 inches, sits in an included plastic stand, and is made in Japan.

The deep, 6-quart sauté pan at the center of the All-Clad NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick VIP comes with a steamer insert, a roasting rack and a tempered glass lid, so one piece of cookware can sear and steam on the stovetop or roast in the oven. The body is hard-anodized recycled aluminum, and a stainless steel base bonded underneath makes it work on induction burners. The ceramic nonstick interior is oven-safe to 450°F, though the lid tops out at 350°F and the pan can’t go under the broiler. Wash it by hand, and know that All-Clad’s warranty on this pan runs one year.

Carbon steel seasons and sears like cast iron, and it heats up and cools down faster when you adjust the burner. Made In’s Seasoned Carbon Steel Frying Pan arrives pre-seasoned with shea nut and coconut oils, so you can start cooking in it sooner than you could with a bare pan. The 12-inch size weighs 4.31 pounds, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2.25-inch sides. Made In builds it in Sweden, rates it for heat up to 1,200°F, and notes it works on induction and over an open fire. The hollow stainless handle is designed to stay cool, and the pan should be washed by hand and dried right away.

Smithey is better known for cast iron, but its Deep Farmhouse Skillet is hand-forged carbon steel, made in Charleston, South Carolina. It’s about 12 inches across the top and 2 inches deep, which leaves room for a pan sauce or a shallow fry, and the cooking surface measures about 9.5 inches. Long handles on both sides stretch it to almost 21 inches end to end, so you can carry all 6 pounds of it to the table with two hands. Smithey lists it for use on gas, induction, electric and open fire.

Industry observers note that smithey’s 7.25 QT Dutch Oven skips enamel entirely. It’s bare cast iron with a fully polished interior, pre-seasoned with grapeseed oil, so it builds up seasoning the same way a skillet does and there’s no enamel coating to chip. The domed lid has drip channels on its underside that send condensation back down onto the food during a long braise. Expect some heft, since it weighs about 17.3 pounds with the lid. Smithey makes it in the US and backs it with a lifetime guarantee. Bare iron doesn’t love long simmers in tomato or wine, so save those braises for an enameled pot or keep them short.

Old cast iron is prized for its smooth, machined cooking surfaces, and Lancaster Cast Iron’s No. 8 Skillet brings that finish to a new pan. The cooking surface is polished smooth, then pre-seasoned with two layers of grapeseed oil at the company’s shop in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The No. 8 measures 10.5 inches across the top, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2-inch walls, and it weighs about 4 pounds. Polished iron starts out slick, and it gets slicker as layers of seasoning build up with every cook.

In a recent development, cooking pancakes in a skillet is a solitary affair. If you’re the cook and don’t want to force cold coasters on everyone, you’re standing alone and eating last. Unless you have this latest griddle, that is. This 12-pound rectangle spans two burners and stays put, providing an 18.5-by-9.8-inch cooking surface and two heat zones, so you can cook a bunch of pancakes, or eggs and bacon, simultaneously, which means everyone eats together. The carbon steel is nitrided, which means it resists rust and scratches without the need for questionable coatings. Plus, it arrives pre-seasoned with a surface that will only become more non-stick with proper use and care. Plus, a raised lip and rounded corners keep grease in while making it easy to pour off. It’s a great choice whether you’re cooking at the stovetop, in an oven, on a grill, or over a campfire.

A saucier’s rounded bottom leaves no corners for a whisk or spatula to miss, which makes it the pan for custard and polenta and anything else that likes to scorch where the wall meets the floor. The Misen 3 QT Stainless Steel Saucier is 5-ply, with aluminum layers sandwiched inside stainless steel to spread heat across the base, and the walls are 3 millimeters thick. It measures about 9 inches across, comes with a lid, works on induction, and is oven-safe to 800°F. Misen backs it with a lifetime warranty against defects.

Sources indicate that kuhn Rikon’s 4th Burner Pot is tall and narrow, 5.5 inches across and holding 12 cups, so it fits on the small back burner while bigger pans take the front of the stove. That makes it handy for a couple of servings of pasta or a batch of blanched green beans. The glass lid has two built-in strainers and a pour spout, which lets you drain without hauling out a colander, and a removable basket inside handles steaming. Interior measurement marks save you a measuring cup, the silicone handles stay cool, and the stainless pot works on induction.

Microwave cooking goes better when steam is managed, and that’s the idea behind the Anyday 8-Piece Glass Round Dish Set. Each borosilicate glass dish gets a tempered glass lid with a silicone vent and gasket that let steam build and escape while the food cooks. Anyday indicates the stainless steel rim on each lid is microwave-safe as long as the dish sits at least an inch from the microwave’s walls. The set includes four dishes: two 4-cup sizes, one shallow and one deep, plus a 7-cup and an 8-cup. The bowls can go in the oven up to 500°F, so leftovers can get a crisp finish after they reheat.

Industry observers note that green tea scorches at a full boil, and pour-over coffee likes water a few degrees below it. The Fellow Corvo EKG Pro lets you dial in anywhere from 104 to 212 degrees Fahrenheit, then hold that temperature for 15 to 60 minutes so the second cup is as hot as the first. It also has an altitude setting, scheduling, and a pre-boil sanitize mode. The 0.9-liter body is 304 stainless steel. Fellow states the Wi-Fi only handles firmware updates, so you’ll still set the temperature on the kettle itself rather than from your phone.

Uneven grounds make uneven coffee, because the fine bits over-extract while the significant chunks barely give up any flavor. The Fellow Ode Brew Grinder Gen 2 uses 64 mm stainless steel flat burrs, which cut a more uniform particle than the blade grinders most people start with. You get 11 settings split into 31 steps, a 100-gram capacity, and anti-static tech to keep grounds from clinging to the catch cup. Fellow built it for drip, pour-over, French press, and cold brew. It isn’t designed for espresso, so skip it for anyone pulling shots at home.

A coffee maker can only brew as well as its water temperature allows. The Moccamaster KBGV Select, handmade in the Netherlands, heats water rapidly to brewing temperature with a copper boiling element, and the hot plate runs on its own separate element so it doesn’t cook the coffee sitting in the carafe. A switch on the brew basket adjusts the flow for a full 10-cup pot or a half batch, which keeps small batches from coming out thin. It carries the Specialty Coffee Association’s certification and a five-year warranty.

It has been revealed that most of the frustration of home espresso comes from dosing and grinding by feel. The Ninja Luxe Café Premier handles both: it has a conical burr grinder with 25 settings and a built-in scale that weighs the grounds for you, so each shot starts from a consistent dose. The Dual Froth System has four hands-free presets for steamed or frothed milk, and the machine also makes drip-style coffee and cold brew. It suits someone who wants café drinks without learning to tamp and time shots by eye.

So you know someone with a grinder, a pour-over cone, a French press, a cold brew pitcher, and a milk frother. But sometimes they need a coffee before they can face making coffee. And that’s where this indulgently overengineered Swiss superautomatic espresso maker comes in. The second-generation Z10 has a menu of 51 drinks you can choose and customize through the 4.3-inch touchscreen. Just pour beans into the hopper and fill the water tank. Drinks include classic hot options, as well as “cold brew,” which, while not true long-immersion, is still nice for ice thanks to unheated water pulsing through a coarser grind. With milk or without. But now there are also light selections, plus caffeine regulation levels, as well as sweet foam picks (with a $35 chocolate attachment sold separately). And the upgraded P.R.G.2+ grinder resets itself for each offering, dialing in optimized granule consistency so you never have to worry you’ll have bad luck with a puck. Sure, it’s a splurge, but think of all the time and space someone will save replacing all those other coffee contraptions.

Most countertop carbonators tell you to fizz plain water and add flavor afterward, because carbonating juice or wine tends to foam over. The Drinkmate OmniFizz gets around that with what the firm calls its Fizz Infuser cap, which releases pressure gradually so you can carbonate cold drinks other than water. It runs on standard 60-liter CO2 cylinders, and Drinkmate sells it alone or in bundles with extra cylinders. Check the bundles before buying, since the kits with more cylinders were sometimes cheaper than the smaller ones in early November.

Recent findings suggest that matcha powder starts losing its color and flavor once it’s ground, which is why the Cuzen Matcha Maker grinds whole tea leaves on demand. Its hopper holds up to 20 grams of leaf, and the machine mills it, then mixes it with water in the cup using a magnetic whisk. You can pick a 1-, 1.5-, or 2-gram shot depending on how strong you like it, and there’s a grind-only mode for baking or lattes. The Starter Kit comes with 4-gram samples of three Cuzen leaf blends and a brush for cleaning the mill.

Pod-based cocktail machines lock you into one company’s drinks. The Barsys 360 uses whatever you put in it: six 750-milliliter canisters hold your own spirits, juices, and syrups, and a Bluetooth app tells the machine how much of each to pour through the spouts over the glass. It doesn’t shake or stir, so strategy on finishing drinks the old-fashioned way. It also runs on USB-C power and weighs about 10 pounds empty, which makes it easier than you’d expect to move from the counter to a party table.

In a recent development, nugget ice, the soft, chewable kind, is made by compressing ice flakes rather than freezing cubes in a tray. The GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro does that on your counter, and Govee rates it for up to 60 pounds a day, with the first batch ready in about six minutes. A 4.9-liter side tank supplements the 2.2-liter main reservoir so you refill less often, and it has two self-cleaning cycles. You can also check on it or start it from the Govee app or by voice with Alexa or Google.

Centrifugal juicers spin produce against a fast blade, while slow juicers like the Hurom H310 Easy Clean press it with a turning screw at roughly 45 rotations per minute. Hurom’s version has a self-feeding hopper with a 50-millimeter chute that the company claims fits whole apples, which cuts down on prep. Hurom backs the 150-watt motor with a 10-year warranty and covers the other parts for two years.

Boxed wine stays fresh longer than an open bottle, but the cardboard box is nobody’s idea of a centerpiece. The Boxxle Box Wine Dispenser is a stainless steel and ABS plastic housing for the bag inside a standard box. According to Boxxle, it lifts the bag so the spout sits above your glass and presses on the bag as it empties, so you can keep pouring until the last glass.

Fresh pasta dough needs to be rolled thin and evenly, and doing it with a rolling pin takes practice most people don’t have. The Marcato Atlas 150 is a hand-cranked roller with a 10-position thickness dial, so you can step the dough down a little at a time until it’s thin enough for lasagna sheets. The rollers are anodized aluminum, and the body is chrome-plated steel made in Italy. The version sold in the US includes fettuccine and spaghetti cutters, so you can go from sheet to noodles without buying attachments.

Recent findings suggest that most stand mixers drive a beater from above. The Ankarsrum Assistent Original flips that: its motor sits in the base and spins the 7-liter stainless steel bowl itself, while a dough hook or roller stays put. That design is why Ankarsrum says it can knead up to 5 kilograms of dough, a load that would stall a lot of tilt-head mixers. The Essential Package comes with a dough roller, dough knife, dough hook, spatula, and a proofing lid. Ankarsrum covers the base with a seven-year warranty, though accessories aren’t included.

Bread machines have a reputation for pale, unevenly baked tops. The Zojirushi Home Bakery Virtuoso Plus adds a heater in the lid to go with the usual one underneath, so the top of the loaf browns along with the sides. It bakes a 2-pound loaf and uses two kneading blades, which helps it work a full 2-pound batch of dough evenly.

Sourdough gets its crackly crust from steam trapped around the loaf early in the bake, which is why so many bakers use a Dutch oven. The Challenger Bread Pan rearranges that idea: you set the dough on a shallow cast-iron base and lower a tall domed lid over it, so you’re not dropping a floppy loaf into a deep, 500-degree pot. It weighs 20 pounds, is made in the USA, and is rated to 500 degrees Fahrenheit. Its 15.5-by-10.5-inch footprint fits oblong batards as well as round boules.

HexClad’s hybrid surface finally made the jump from frying pans to the oven. The HexClad Hybrid Baking Sheets use the same pattern of raised stainless steel hexagons with nonstick valleys in between, built over 2.5-millimeter tri-ply with an aluminum core. HexClad states the ceramic coating is free of PFAS and rates the sheets for oven temperatures up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re sold in two-packs in small and medium sizes, and the medium sheet measures 10 by 15 inches. HexClad says they’re dishwasher-safe but recommends washing them by hand.

Detroit-style pizza owes its crunchy, cheese-crisped edges to a deep rectangular pan that conducts heat fast. The LloydPans 10×14 Detroit-Style Pizza Pan is 2.5 inches deep and made from 14-gauge anodized aluminum in Spokane Valley, Washington. Its Pre-Seasoned Tuff-Kote finish means you can skip seasoning and use metal utensils on it, according to LloydPans. Spread the cheese all the way to the edges so it melts down the sides and fries against the metal.

Industry observers note that stretching pizza dough on a countertop usually ends with flour everywhere. The Gozney Pizza Prep Board has raised edges that keep the flour on the board and a catch tray at the back where you can sweep extra flour and reuse it. Its textured surface holds a thin, even coating of flour, which Gozney says works better than wood, steel, or marble at keeping dough from sticking and tearing on its way to the peel. A bench hook keeps it from sliding, and size markings go up to 16 inches. It’s 22 by 21.5 inches, so check counter space first.

According to recent reports, neapolitan pizza wants a stone near 850 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature home ovens don’t reach. The Ooni Volt 2, successor to the Volt 12, gets there on a standard 120-volt outlet in about 20 minutes, according to Ooni. Inside is a 10-millimeter cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pizzas, and Ooni’s Pizza Intelligence system shifts power between the heating elements as you cook. Presets cover Neapolitan, thin and crispy, and pan pizza. At about 39 pounds, it’s heavy enough that you’ll want to give it a permanent spot.

Sources indicate that chef Nancy Silverton started with a quarter sheet pan when she helped Made In design this dish, then stretched it longer and wider. The Made In Porcelain Baking Slab is a 9-by-13-inch French porcelain dish fired three times in the Loire Valley, with a lower profile than a typical casserole so roasted vegetables and gratins get more browning. It’s oven-safe to 650 degrees Fahrenheit and microwave-safe, and it weighs 3.8 pounds. Made In’s care guide indicates it can go in the dishwasher, though the firm’s FAQ recommends hand washing.

Most microwaves cook by guesswork, and the most interaction you have is five beeps and the sighs/screams when things are too cold in the middle and hot at the edges. This sleek Japanese Microwave from Panasonic, however, uses its fresh Genius Sensor 2.0 to constantly measure 64 points on your food’s surface every 0.1 seconds, so one button push can achieve even temperature throughout a plate of mixed leftovers. And steady inverter power ensures the center heats, too. The drop-down door, like a wall oven, suits even a narrow galley kitchen (aka many Asian apartments), while the flat, turntable-free interior can fit up to a 9-by-13 dish. This recent import is a 2026 Red Dot Design winner for a reason: it’s got a look as tasty as your bowl of steamy soup.

Recent findings suggest that want that perfectly fluffy restaurant rice at home, but without under- or over-cooking anxiety and hot-spot drama? Get a Zojirushi rice cooker. I’ve given the NS-ZCC10 Neuro Fuzzy Logic model as a graduation/housewarming gift multiple times because I knew from personal experience it delivers year after year. Then I got this pressure + induction cooker in 2025 and daaaaaaamn … somehow the best got better. Sticky-plump sushi or stir-fry grains, pleasingly textured oatmeal, brown rice that doesn’t take all of eternity. No sad, beige cement. This tiny, calm chef quietly adjusts the heat to deliver evenly cooked everything. It’s not as fast as some cookers, but it beats them in consistency. Fill to the line, press a button, go live life, come back to perfection. This is an upgrade that quietly, magically improves your entire kitchen rhythm.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve wasted so many herbs. You buy basil with such good intentions, but two recipes and three days later, there’s still so much that’s wilted and wasted. Same can be mentioned for other greens. And maybe you know someone in the same situation. One “simple” solution is for them to grow their own greens, but not everyone has room for a garden. And what about winter … Well, that’s where this egg-shaped enclosure comes in. Using NASA-inspired nutrient-infused fogponics (way more exciting to watch than standard hydroponics), anyone can grow lettuce or kale or cherry tomatoes, etc., from pre-seeded pods/reusable germination domes, and do it year-round. Just put the indoor garden in a side room, garage, basement, etc., (grow lights can get pretty bright), connect it to Wi-Fi with the Plantaform app, and give it water when an alert tells you. Then, in a few weeks, harvest time! Seasonings season! Garnishes galore! Just clean it well, and you’ll be able to keep good produce on the cutting board, not in the compost. Literally rinse and repeat.

Coffee nerds have so much in common with audiophiles. Both are obsessed with micro-calibrated gear and swapping components in and out in the pursuit of clarity. So if you know someone as obsessed with puck preparation as they are running a carbon-fiber anti-static brush over every album, you know someone who needs the Mazzer Philos premium light commercial single-dose grinder. Like a summit-fi digital audio converter, this $1,495 hand-assembled, heirloom-quality Italian appliance (available in black and silver) takes whatever beans it’s fed and extracts previously masked tasting notes with minimal morning commotion. A wide dial covers espresso to pour-over to batch brew coarseness, and the near-zero-retention vertical burr + chute knocker + Dose Finisher system lets you move between origins and brewing methods without yesterday’s beans staging a comeback. Swappable 64mm flat burrs give someone a chance to tune for vibrant light and full-bodied dark roasts, and the option to switch from stepped to stepless mode gives grind settings the same obsessive precision as establishing the perfect listening position.

In a recent development, south Korea isn’t a casual getaway. But you can still get some Seoul in your soul (food) at home with this set of sauces from three-Michelin-star chef Mingoo Kang of Mingles restaurant and James Beard Award winner Nadia Cho. Fermented slowly in onggi (traditional Korean clay jars that are buried in the hills), and branded with the Korean word for artisan, these sauces are so much better than the red plastic tub of industrial soybean-chili paste you’d pick up at the store (but I still got love for you, H Mart). Start by stirring the deep heat of cooking sauce into marinades, dressings, and/or broths, then use the finishing sauce to glaze meats, or drizzle some zest onto eggs, rice, or dumplings. Whether a chef you know prefers marinara or bibimbap, give them the gift of earthenware alchemy.

Nik Sharma’s newest book builds its 100 recipes around the science of flavor, explaining why each technique works. Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking came out from Chronicle Books in September 2026. It’s a good fit for the cook who keeps asking why a recipe calls for a specific step, and wants the answer along with dinner.

GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a upcoming study.
  • Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.
  • They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a upcoming study.

Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 people also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

It has been revealed that “The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” stated Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”.

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he noted.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but mentioned the findings were “quite impressive.”.

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are key factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

It has been revealed that for their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

It has been revealed that the researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Sources indicate that eckel remarked in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an vital finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel noted in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management challenges.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

It has been revealed that “They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler mentioned. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Among those lifestyle modifications are:.

Cutler said the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most important thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he said.

It’s a little extra maintenance, sure, but worthwhile if you’re investing this much in a pair of boots.

Tech Report: The 'Possibility Couple' Is a Gen Z Dating Trend

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • It has been revealed that so, say you want to be one half of a power couple—you know, a romantic pairing where both of you are successful and influential like Beyoncé and Jay-Z or Mr.
  • It has been revealed that well, how about trying to be part of a "possibility couple" now?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

It has been revealed that so, say you want to be one half of a power couple—you know, a romantic pairing where both of you are successful and influential like Beyoncé and Jay-Z or Mr. and Mrs. Incredible. But the problem is you are still early on in your own personal power trip—meaning that you yourself have not become successful yet. What then can you do?

It has been revealed that well, how about trying to be part of a "possibility couple" now? That's a pairing that's all about the P's—namely "potential," "possibilities", "prediction," "potent," and, yes, maybe "power" eventually. A "possibility couple" is one that doesn't have power per se at the present. But it's got the potential to become quite potent in the future. In other words, based on what you are seeing now, you predict that together you'll have lots of potent possibilities down the road.

Recent findings suggest that it shouldn't be super-surprising that the "possibility couple" is central to Hinge's third annual Gen Z D.A.T.E. (Data, Advice, Trends, and Expertise) Report titled: “Dating While Dreaming Big.” Since Gen Zers are those born between 1997 and 2012, they are now no older than 29 and thus are mostly still in the fruitcake batter stages of their lives—still forming their identities and possibilities.

The Hinge report hinged on surveys administered to the over 13,000 owners of the dating app. The survey results did suggest that many Gen Z respondents are looking into the future when evaluating their present dating prospects. For example, 81 percent of Gen Z respondents felt that "ending up with their ideal partner would make achieving their ideal life more likely," and 67 percent "would prefer a partner who makes them feel hopeful and inspired over someone who simply fits the life they’re already building." This forward-oriented view seemed to be more present among the Gen Zers, with 76 percent of them vs. 65 percent of millennials saying that "when they imagine their ideal romantic partner, they’re also imagining the person they want to become.".

Sources indicate that none of these are terrible things. Thinking more about your future and playing more of a long game when dating can be good approaches. The opposite would be just considering the here and now and trying to satisfy your immediate urges, such as, "Sure, that person is a bit crazy but so, so hot, and I'm so, so horny." Focusing too much on the present when looking for a partner can be like buying a pair of low-riding skinny jeans and thinking, "I'm going to wear these for life.".

It has been revealed that when you think only about who you are right now, rather than who you might become, you could be destined for some D's—meaning dispute, despair, and potentially divorce. You could end up outgrowing the other person. Or the person could end up holding you back. So, yes, it does make sense to find a person who is more open to possibilities for both of you.

Recent findings suggest that A seemingly big challenge, though, of finding a possibility pairing is having to P a lot—meaning predicting, projecting, and prognosticating. It's not like a potential power pairing, where you can simply say, "I got the power. Do you?" and find the answer to be "yes" in both of your eyes. Whether the two of you might last without an eventual power outage is a different story.

In a recent development, with a "possibility couple, any potential projections are further complicated by having to prognosticate for not just one but both of you when you don't know each other very well. In fact, neither of you may even be that self-aware yet. Plus, as stock market investors, weather forecasters, and the makers of Crystal Pepsi, Segways, and Joker: Folie à Deux will tell you, predicting what will happen in the future is not easy.

Recent findings suggest that sure, there are present-day signs. For example, someone at the moment in law school is very likely to become a lawyer in a few years. But that lawyer could easily one day say, "Forget the law. Bring on yarn bombing." And who knows what twists and turns life may bring, such as health challenges, unexpected people entering or exiting, workplace and industry overhauls, or encountering a life-changing piece of tiramisu. I have previously warned in "A Funny Bone to Pick" about the dangers of dating someone's potential future self rather than who the person currently is because that person may end up never changing.

Industry observers note that therefore, the best possibility might be to balance the present with the future. You can ask yourself the question that I've already posed for "A Funny Bone to Pick"—namely, are you stronger with or without the person? Look for qualities that potential partners already have that would project well into the future.

One such quality is open-mindedness—being open to different possibilities and people. After all, you may become a very different person at least outwardly. So, beware of anyone who stereotypes, focuses too much on superficial things, and holds strong biases.

Sources indicate that A second quality is adaptability—the ability to accommodate future changes, such as the two of you growing in different ways. Or is your potential partner more like a starched denim thong—rigid and inflexible in a way that's surely going to drive a wedge between you in the future?

Thirdly, do they even want you to succeed and have a true teammate mindset where they want their partner to be as potent as possible? Or must they outshine everyone, including you? Beware of the people who make themselves feel high by keeping those around them low.

Finally, are they a match for what's inside you—your core, your core personality and values, what won't change over time? If the two of you are attracted to each other's hot legs, abs, job, wallet, memberships, pick-up lines, car, or cast-iron cookware, remember those things definitely change over time—with the possible exception of the cast-iron cookware.

By contrast, what allows for growth is having strong roots beneath the surface. If the two of you can connect those roots—those things that go beyond the superficial—then the resulting possibilities could be endless.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home. In this region in the middle of the Sahara Desert about the size of Switzerland, the olive baboons (Papio anubis) have lived a separate life away from other primate species. At 40 to 60 pounds, some olive baboons are about the size of our early hominin ancestors. But their size does not keep them safe from hungry Verreaux’s eagles (Aquila verreauxii).

Recent findings suggest that new research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons. The discovery is reshaping how scientists think about predator-prey interactions during human evolution.

Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, significant cats, and even eagles. However, scientists believed that our species (Homo sapiens) and our hominin ancestors have been escaping these predators for roughly the past 2.5 million years. No primate over 28.6 pounds (13 kilograms) has been confirmed to be killed by raptors, so our body sizes appeared to be too heavy for even the large eagles with a 71- to 86-inch-long wingspan to pick up.

According to recent reports, in this study, the team describes skulls and bones of adult male olive baboons that bear the signature marks of eagle predation. There were talon punctures to the skulls, and various scrapes and “rakes” on the shoulder bones.

According to recent reports, “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Catherine Hobaiter, a study co-author and primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, said in a statement. “Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

In a recent development, with these remains, the team was able to calculate how much the deceased baboons weighed. One individual was over 57.3 pounds (26 kilograms), well within the range of a hominin species.

“Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence,” added Dr. Jean Didier Akpona from the African Parks Network. “This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”.

It has been revealed that to defend against eagles, our primate ancestors would “mob” or charge the attacker to try to drive them away. The modern primates living in places with eagle predators often move in large groups mixed with other primate species. This also mirrors the evolutionary history of our early ancestors, who lived alongside other hominin species and other primates. While some conflict arose, plenty of cooperative advantages to sticking together also happened—like mobbing eagles.

The team hopes to learn more about the lives of the Ennedi baboons to see what other evolutionary secrets they may be holding.

“Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what fresh ‘rules’ they’ll break next!” Hobaiter concluded.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.
  • Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.
  • Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this new study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

The participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

The low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

Sources indicate that in the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

It has been revealed that this second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

At the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

Sources indicate that “This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

According to recent reports, cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he said.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing concern worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

Sources indicate that research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

People diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:.

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen’s revived Scout brand finally has vehicles coming off the line in South Carolina, but they’re validation units, not customer cars. Scout confirms the first deliveries of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup won’t happen until 2028.

That’s two years later than the 2026 production start the manufacturer was talking about before it even broke ground on its $2 billion factory.

In a recent development, according to Scout’s announcement dated November 12, construction at the Production Center north of Columbia is in its final phase and most of the manufacturing equipment is installed. The Body Shop, Paint Shop, and Assembly Shop are all being used for the first validation builds.

The Body Shop is the most automated part of the plant. Scout indicates more than 750 robots join roughly 160 parts into each body, laying down about 5,000 weld points per vehicle, with AI-supported weld monitoring and a metrology system checking the results. At full capacity, the shop is designed to handle about 40 vehicles per hour.

Bodies then go through an electrified paint shop before landing in final assembly, where they’re married to the chassis and get their wiring, glass, seats, and wheels.

CEO Scott Keogh is clearly happy to have something physical to point to, saying that “what we are building in Blythewood is no longer a promise on paper.”.

Scout also shared photos of a Terra pickup and a Traveler parked inside the plant. Its own fine print notes that they show “concept and validation vehicles” with optional features, so don’t read too much into what’s on display:.

Fair enough. But Scout is also careful about what this stage is. Teams are confirming the equipment is installed and works, and checking engineering, buildability, and parts maturity. Process validation and scaling up to production speed come later. Validation builds will continue “into 2027,” followed by pre-production builds, and then customer deliveries in 2028.

The firm claims the plant will create more than 4,000 jobs, and it’s spending another $300 million on an onsite supplier park expected to support about 1,000 supplier jobs.

It has been revealed that when Keogh laid out the blueprint in late 2023, Scout noted it would start production in 2026 with deliveries shortly after. That was still the target when Scout broke ground in Blythewood in February 2024.

Recent findings suggest that by the Traveler and Terra unveiling in October 2024, production had moved to 2027. Keogh then said in March that he expects the first customer to get a vehicle “sometime in 2028,” and that’s now the official line in Scout’s own press materials.

It might not even be the end of it. Industry forecaster AutoForecast Solutions has the Traveler starting production in September 2028 and the Terra in March 2030. Scout hasn’t confirmed those dates, but it hasn’t given more precise ones either.

The product itself has also changed under the hood. Scout debuted as a pure EV brand, then added the “Harvester” range-extender option at the reveal. According to Keogh, Scout has more than 160,000 reservations, and 87% of them are for the gas-generator version. Those are $100 refundable reservations, not orders.

Der Spiegel reported earlier this year that integrating the range extender, which wasn’t part of the original strategy, was among the technical problems pushing the timeline back.

For comparison, Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019 and delivered the first ones four years later, a delay that was widely mocked. Scout is now on a similar four-year path from reveal to customer, and that’s for the SUV it’s launching first.

In a recent development, A working body shop with 750 robots isn’t vaporware. Scout has a real factory, a real workforce, and two vehicles that people clearly want. 160,000 reservations is a big number for a brand that hasn’t sold a single vehicle in 46 years.

In a recent development, but validation builds are an early step, not a finish line. Scout still has to go through pre-production, prove its processes, and ramp to rate, and every one of those stages is where newly introduced automakers usually lose time. Rivian and Lucid both learned that the hard way.

According to recent reports, september 28? So we're 23 months away? I'm surprised the validation build yadda yadda stuff is supposed to take so long. It's not like VW doesn't know how to do this stuff, and that's a lot of money and equipment to sit mostly idle while 180,000 reservations holders are waiting for their cars. Maybe they're waiting for the market to change or are considering a whole other brand or product line?

In a recent development, and the market Scout was designed for in 2022 no longer exists. The EV tax credit is gone, and most of Scout’s own reservation holders picked the gas generator. In the US, the range-extender market is still early, unlike in China, where they are already popular.

But by 2028, Ford, Ram, and Jeep all strategy to have range-extended trucks and SUVs on sale. Scout’s main advantage was being early with a cool, rugged, American-built electric truck. That advantage shrinks every quarter.

According to recent reports, we’re still rooting for these vehicles. The Traveler and Terra are among the best-looking designs in the segment. But a $100 reservation is easy to walk away from, and the question is how many of those 160,000 people are still waiting in 2028.

#52476. Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1727 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week?
  • It has been revealed that today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty.
  • Recent findings suggest that for most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your fresh favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

It has been revealed that today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

Recent findings suggest that for most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”.

Recent findings suggest that you might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered glitch, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

In a recent development, so when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Industry observers note that ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

The options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.).

The solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

It has been revealed that harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

These days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

It has been revealed that because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

If you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

According to recent reports, opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

Sources indicate that maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

The idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he said, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.).

In the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

It has been revealed that george Papanicolaou moved to New York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

It has been revealed that his wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”.

In 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

It took Stockard’s death, a new boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

Industry News: The Robert Pattinson James Bond Primer

💡 Key Takeaways
  • IN THE TWO weeks since Robert Pattinson’s name was first mentioned in connection with James Bond—and in the handful of days since he was officially cast in the role—I’ve heard lots of talk about him as an actor, and him as a fit playing 007.
  • According to recent reports, these have been some of the easiest conversations I’ve had all year long, because, quite simply, Pattinson has been one of the best actors working for the last decade and counting.
  • But I also recognize that not everyone is grinding out the indies from this year or the hidden gems from that year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IN THE TWO weeks since Robert Pattinson’s name was first mentioned in connection with James Bond—and in the handful of days since he was officially cast in the role—I’ve heard lots of talk about him as an actor, and him as a fit playing 007.

According to recent reports, these have been some of the easiest conversations I’ve had all year long, because, quite simply, Pattinson has been one of the best actors working for the last decade and counting. While his first big breaks came in the commendable space of films based on YA books (Harry Potter and Twilight), he’s long established himself at this point as an actor who can just about do it all, taking on a mix of projects big and small, characters good and evil. He’s shown a full capability run the full gauntlet from sane and noble to absolutely psychotic.

But I also recognize that not everyone is grinding out the indies from this year or the hidden gems from that year. Not everyone is even seeing the movies that some of us think of as the huge movies that everyone saw. But James Bond Casting is the kind of news everyone hears. And so I wanted to do my part to make sure everyone knows one thing only: Robert Pattinson rules.

In a recent development, truly. There’s a common description for many cool actors: “He’s a character actor in a leading man’s body.” And no one seems more true to that than Pattinson, as his jawline cut from marble is often put to work in playing some of the most twisted and eccentric characters you’ll see in any movie. Hell, in 2026 alone, he’s already played a groom-to-be from hell in The Drama, a scheming villain in The Odyssey, and an ambitious 2000s television personality (a.k.a. To Catch a Predator’s Chris Hansen) in Primetime. And that’s not even to mention his role as the villain in Dune: Part Three (from his future Bond director Denis Villeneuve) coming later this year.

But that’s the glory of Pattinson, too—he clearly loves doing all that stuff, but he’s still the dashingly handsome, arrestingly charming guy on the surface, too. It’s a rare combination that makes him a unique star for our times; and clearly the major studios agree, as he’s now been cast as two of contemporary movie culture’s most famous recurring roles, Batman and James Bond.

He’s got a ton of great movies on his resume, ranging from blockbusters to little-seen independents, and almost all are worth your time. He’s even got small roles in some movies—like when he plays a professional driver for Julianne Moore in David Cronenberg’s Maps to the Stars—where he pops even as he tries to keep things grounded.

Sources indicate that but I tried to keep it simple and get you ready for what makes him one of our very best, and a truly inspired Bond pick. So I stuck with six movies. That’s not too bad, right? A six-movie watchlist. Once you watch these six, you’ll get what you need to get about Robert Pattinson—and why he’s both one of the best actors working today, and a slam-dunk pick to play James Bond.

Pattinson went through a complicated process to become Bond that may or may not have involved being paid $1 million just to audition... but you can basically consider his role in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet as his first audition, and one all of us get to see. Nolan’s time-traveling espionage caper is a cool, sleek thriller that’s also a fast-paced battle to keep up with—and Pattinson’s Neil is the cool-as-a-cucumber agent who knows how to keep the whole thing grounded. He’s got great chemistry with the film’s lead, John David Washington, which may even give you ideas on how a Bond and Felix Leiter partnership could work out in a future film. Tenet is an extremely cool movie, and Pattinson is somehow the coolest thing about it.

Also see: Cosmopolis, probably Netflix’s The Take in early 2027.

It has been revealed that while Pattinson has been doing impressive work for basically his whole career (even check out Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire!), it was Good Time—from directors Josh and Benny Safdie—that helped a lot of people in the moviegoing community wake up to just how good he’d become. This million-mile-a-minute crime story follows Connie (Pattinson) as he runs around in the seedy underbelly of Newly introduced York City looking for money to bail him out of one terrible situation after another. In other words... it’s a Safdie movie. If you want to see how a Pattinson Bond could look as he deals with a mission gone awry or some other massive fuck-up, this is your movie.

It’s not easy to put a whole movie on your back—and it’s even harder when it’s something that comes with massive expectations. In 2022’s The Batman, Pattinson became the latest actor to put his spin on Gotham City’s cave-dwelling vigilante, and, in typical Pattinson fashion, made him a character all his own. Where Pattinson shines is in the care he puts into both the Batman and Bruce Wayne personas; his early-career Batman is basically an ass-kicking noir detective, while his Bruce Wayne is kind of a brooding emo rich kid. The whole movie rocks, essentially a three-hour crime epic—but it’s easy to see why Amazon-MGM and director Denis Villeneuve felt comfortable putting their franchise on Pattinson’s bat armor-covered back.

Pattinson has also put in a lot of time playing creeps. In The Lighthouse, he plays a man stuck spending time with a grumpy, farting Willem Dafoe, and who eventually falls into his own descent, killing people and seagulls alike. And, well, he’s just not a great guy. Pattinson’s willingness to lose himself in a role, putting that psychosis front and center for all to see, marks an impressive willingness to both not be the hero, and to be vulnerable—which can also be great tools for someone as layered and complex as Bond tends to be.

Also see: The Odyssey, The Devil All the Time.

According to recent reports, there’s another hallmark of Pattinson’s recent work: playing characters who, at one point or another, reveal themself to be freaky little freaks. Sometimes, like in James Gray’s The Lost City of Z, that’s evident from the jump, as he plays a bespectacled, bearded oddball. Other times, like in The Drama—which came out earlier this year and was a major hit for A24—he appears to be relatively normal at first, before eventually putting his antisocial behavior or extreme neuroses on display. The Drama is a wonderful character study, with Pattinson and Zendaya bouncing off each other marvelously, and it’s a thrill to watch Pattinson’s devolution into weirdo in a story that feels decidedly of the present. James Bond is a sleek, cool, spy, sure, but you don’t cast Robert Pattinson to just be a sleek, cool spy. Hopefully there’s a way for him to tap into his freak bona fides.

Also see: The Lost City of Z, Probably Dune: Part Three.

It has been revealed that if you want to see Pattinson’s ability to be purely magnetic on screen, Primetime is the movie. Director Lance Oppenheim’s narrative debut is a thrilling and darkly comedic portrayal of ambition in the post-9/11 age of mid-aughts TV, and Pattinson leads the way as NBC’s Chris Hansen. He absolutely crushes every aspect of the role, making tens of choices with every single line and eating them all up like he’s at an all-you-can-eat buffet. He also bounces masterfully off costars Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. The character is huge, narcissistic, and borderline evil, but Pattinson’s real skill is on display in making Hanson still never feel quite less than human. That’s a tricky balance beam to walk—but one he always manages to make look effortless.

According to recent reports, general Motors is looking for a latest captain to steer the organization, according to a story published on November 17 in the Wall Street Journal. The company is reportedly preparing for a future without CEO Mary Barra, who has led the automotive giant through a myriad of tumultuous times since taking the helm in 2014.

Industry observers note that according to the WSJ report, GM is working with an executive search firm in an effort to identify potential outside candidates to succeed Barra. That remarked, the tech giant has not publicly commented on when the executive could step aside.
